---

## Angle 1 — Correctness and regression

**🔴 Dead responsive-image pipeline — mega-menu/drawer promo images ship unoptimized. CONFIRMED, ONE-OFF.**
`overrides/app/utils/contentfulImage.ts` defines `buildContentfulResponsiveImage`/`ContentfulResponsiveImage` — a fully-built, heavily-documented AVIF/WebP responsive-srcset builder whose own doc comment says it's "used for the header mega-menu's promo images (desktop/tablet: `megaMenuContent/index.tsx`, mobile drawer L2: `drawer-menu/index.tsx`)". I grepped every consumer:
```
grep -rln "buildContentfulResponsiveImage|ContentfulResponsiveImage|avifSrcSet|webpSrcSet" overrides/app/components
→ (no results)
```
Both actual call sites render a plain, unoptimized image instead:
- `overrides/app/components/list-menu/megaMenuContent/index.tsx:152`: `<Image src={promoImage.src} alt={promoImage.alt} loading="lazy" __css={styles.promoImage} />`
- `overrides/app/components/drawer-menu/index.tsx:223`: same pattern.

`promoImage.src` comes straight from `resolveImageEntry.ts:29` (`asset.fields.file.url`) — the raw Contentful CDN URL, no `w=`/`fm=avif`/`q=` params at all. The display box is not a thumbnail either — `megaMenuContent.css.ts`'s own comment cites a fixed 862px-wide `promoImageWrapper`. This directly contradicts AGENTS.md's Performance section ("serve correctly sized images... never render full-resolution images at thumbnail size") and the utility's own stated purpose. `contentfulImage.test.ts` passes fine in isolation — this is exactly the class of gap unit tests and `tsc`/lint cannot see.

**🟡 Mega-menu can get stuck open with a phantom "Close" control after a rapid hover→close. PLAUSIBLE, ONE-OFF.**
Traced through `useMegaMenuMotion.ts`'s reducer + `list-menu-popover.tsx`'s `useTransitionSafeValue`:
- `useTransitionSafeValue` (list-menu-popover.tsx:38-57) defers committing a new CSS target value by two `requestAnimationFrame`s, so a genuine prior painted frame exists before the value changes (this is a real, previously-confirmed empirical fix, well documented).
- `useMegaMenuMotion`'s `CLOSE` handler, when `state.phase === 'expanding'`, jumps straight to `{...state, phase: 'collapsing', pendingItemId: null}` (useMegaMenuMotion.ts:65-67) — **keeping `activeItemId`** — specifically to dodge a different, already-guarded stuck-transition bug (contentOut never fading because opacity was never visible). This case *is* covered by an explicit regression test (`useMegaMenuMotion.test.ts:162`, "closing mid-expand collapses directly instead of routing through contentOut").
- But if `CLOSE` fires *before* the original HOVER's deferred double-rAF has committed `value = '1fr'` (i.e., within ~2 animation frames of the hover), `gridTemplateRowsTarget` recomputes to `'0fr'` — which is **already** the current, uncommitted `value`. `setValue('0fr')` is then a no-op (React bails on an identical value), so `grid-template-rows` never actually changes, no CSS transition runs, `onTransitionEnd` never fires, and `COLLAPSE_COMPLETE` is never dispatched. The phase machine is stuck at `'collapsing'` with `activeItemId` still set — so `ListMenuView`'s `useEffect` (list-menu.tsx:59-65) never calls `reportClose()`, and the header shell's `isMegaMenuOpen` stays `true`, keeping `RightBar` on its `'fullSwap'` Close-control (rightBar/index.tsx:175-185) instead of search/icons.
- Real trigger: opening a mega-menu item and closing it (Escape, or `ListMenuTrigger`'s own `onKeyDown` Escape handler at `list-menu-trigger.tsx:72`) within a couple of frames — plausible via a fast Enter-then-Escape keyboard sequence, not just an implausible mouse micro-movement.
- It's self-healing on the *next* hover — the reducer's `HOVER` handler explicitly treats a stuck `'collapsing'` phase as a fresh open (`useMegaMenuMotion.ts:43`) — but in the interim the header shows a stale "Close" control with no visible menu. None of `useMegaMenuMotion.test.ts`'s 14 reducer-only tests exercise this because the bug lives one layer down, in the DOM-timing interaction the reducer tests can't see.

**🟡 `useHeaderNav`'s documented fetch-failure behaviour is wrong, unread, and untested. CONFIRMED, ONE-OFF.**
`overrides/app/hooks/useHeaderNav.ts:45-49`'s `@returns` doc says `items` is `undefined` "on fetch failure... callers should treat that the same as 'nothing to render yet'" — but the type doc four lines above it (line 20-23) and the actual implementation (line 78-82: `items = isLoading ? undefined : resolved ? filterByRegion(...) : []`) agree that `items` is **always `[]`, never `undefined`, once `isLoading` is false** — including on error. Neither `list-menu.tsx:165` nor `drawer-menu/index.tsx:255` ever reads `isError` at all (confirmed by grep — the only non-mock occurrence of `isError` anywhere in the new code is a mocked value in two test files). `useHeaderNav.test.ts`'s 5 tests cover success/empty/locale-fallback but never mock a rejected `getEntries()` call, so this contradiction was never caught. Functionally this likely still fails closed acceptably (empty nav, no crash), but the doc is actively wrong and the failure path is unverified.

---

## Angle 2 — Conventions, structure, and tier ownership

**🔴/flag — Tier 1 `theme/foundation/` files modified. CONFIRMED (the edit); NOT independently verifiable (the sign-off).**
`overrides/app/theme/foundation/gridSystem.ts` and `overrides/app/theme/foundation/zimmTokens.ts` are both edited by this PR (commit `9a1d3d9`, "centralize outer container padding into gridSystem.ts"). Both are listed verbatim under Tier 1 "Design System (Owner: UI Designer)" in `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md`, and AGENTS.md Hard Rule #3 says this folder specifically requires UI-designer sign-off. The change itself is well-engineered (derives `containerPadding` from `spacing.ts` instead of hardcoding, adds a `grid.maxWidth` token, backed by a matching `theme/index.test.tsx` update) and its comment claims "confirmed with the design team 2026-08-27" — but that's a code comment, not a recorded approval, and I found no reference to designer sign-off in the commit message itself. This needs to be confirmed as a process fact before merge; I can't settle it from the diff.

**🟡 Stale "not wired" documentation across 3 files — contradicted by this PR's own code. CONFIRMED, UNIFORM (same stale claim, 4 separate spots).**
`header/headerTypes.ts:17-21`'s `MenuExpandedState` doc, `header/leftBar/index.tsx:19` (`menuExpanded` prop) and `:23` (`onBack` prop), and `header/rightBar/index.tsx:79-80` (`menuExpanded`) and `:84` (`onClose`) all say variants of "Not wired to any real mega-menu/drawer state on this branch... is that follow-up work's job (SFCC-96/97)." But `header/index.tsx:156-203` in this *same* PR demonstrably wires real state: `useHeaderMenuExpandedState` (a genuine depth state machine) and `isMegaMenuOpen`/`MegaMenuOpenContext` (genuinely driven by `ListMenuView`'s `activeItemId`, confirmed via `list-menu.tsx:58-65`) both feed the real `menuExpanded` value passed to `LeftBar`/`RightBar`. These comments are leftovers from an earlier point in the 65-commit history that never got reconciled with the later wiring work.

**🔵 Stale comment claims `navGroup.js` doesn't exist yet — it does, in this same PR. CONFIRMED.**
`scripts/contentful/content-types/headerNavItem.js:29-31`: "`navGroup` is authored on a separate branch... and has no local file in this content-types/ directory yet." `scripts/contentful/content-types/navGroup.js` is a complete, 36-line file created by this PR. Same root cause as the finding above.

**🔵 Out-of-scope drive-by edit. CONFIRMED.**
`overrides/app/constants/index.ts` gains one line unrelated to the header rebuild: `* TODO: Review this file and remove any constants that are not used.` Trivial, but it's scope creep in the license-header block of an already very large PR, against AGENTS.md's "Minimal changes" rule.

**Could not verify — Squad A/B coordination.** `squadA.md` requires notifying Squad B before touching `header/`, `footer/`, `drawer-menu/`, `list-menu/`. Whether that happened isn't visible in the code or git history I have access to.

---

## Angle 3 — Contract fidelity

**🔴 New barrel file re-exports the base (unstyled) `ListMenuPopover` instead of this PR's own override. CONFIRMED, ONE-OFF (but a repeatable-shape landmine).**
`overrides/app/components/list-menu/index.ts` is a brand-new file (confirmed: doesn't exist at `269d5d4`). Line 3:
```ts
export { ListMenuPopover } from '@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/list-menu/list-menu-popover';
```
This PR *also* creates a full local override at `overrides/app/components/list-menu/list-menu-popover.tsx` (282 lines) specifically to fix base `ListMenuPopover`'s internal relative-import of the base (inaccessible) `list-menu-trigger` — but the barrel still points at the base path instead of `./list-menu-popover`. Live impact today is contained — `list-menu.tsx:3` (the real consumer) correctly imports the override via the relative path, sidestepping the broken barrel — but the barrel is the one place the SFCC-bridge pattern says a downstream consumer *should* be able to trust. Per `package.json`'s `"ccExtensibility": {"extends": "@salesforce/retail-react-app", "overridesDir": "overrides"}` (whole-package path mirroring, not per-directory registration), this would still resolve correctly in the real webpack build, but per `overrideStyling.md`'s own documented gotcha, Storybook and Vitest don't run that resolver — so any future story/test that imports `ListMenuPopover` the "normal" way (via the barrel, the pattern the codebase's own docs recommend) would silently exercise the unstyled base component. This is the same defect class as the codebase's already-acknowledged `product-tile`/`DisplayPrice` instance — this PR adds a second one. `overrides/app/components/list-menu/index.ts:4`'s `ListMenuContent` re-export from base is, by contrast, correct (no local override exists for it) — included for contrast, not as a finding.

**Clean — DrawerMenu/ListMenu default-export API compatibility.** Both accept every prop base `_app/index.jsx` passes (`root`, `itemsKey`, `itemsCountKey`, `itemComponent`/`contentComponent`) even though they ignore most of them, per their own documented "self-fetches its own data" design (`drawer-menu/index.tsx:236-238`, `list-menu.tsx:148-151`). No crash risk found.

---

## Angle 4 — Failure modes and security

- No `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` anywhere in the new header/nav/drawer/mega-menu code (grep confirmed zero hits).
- `isSafeHref` (pre-existing, reused correctly) gates every Contentful-sourced `href` through `ZimmNavItem` (`zimmNavItem/index.tsx:100`), failing closed to a non-navigating `<button>` on an unsafe scheme.
- 🔵 **Note, defense-in-depth**: `scripts/contentful/content-types/headerNavItem.js:27`'s `href` field is a free-text `Symbol` with no CMS-side pattern validation — the *only* defense against a `javascript:`-scheme href is the frontend's `isSafeHref`. That defense does work today, but there's no belt-and-braces at the content-authoring layer.
- `useContentfulClient.ts`'s new try/catch around `getContentfulConfig()` (for Storybook's non-SSR context) and `useHeaderNav`'s `enabled: !!client` gate together mean a missing/broken Contentful config never throws — it degrades to an empty nav. Consistent with AGENTS.md's "each external system must fail independently."

---

## Angle 5 — Token and styling strategy

**Semantic-intent check: clean.** Spot-checked every new recipe (`header.css.ts`, `leftBar.css.ts`, `rightBar.css.ts`, `zimmNavItem.css.ts`, `zimmSearchInput.css.ts`, `megaMenuContent.css.ts`, `list-menu.css.ts`, `drawer-menu.css.ts`) — every `text.*`/`icon.*` var is on `color:`, every `bg`/`background.*` var is on `background`/`bg`, `border.*` vars (e.g. `zimmSearchInput.css.ts:25`'s `var(--zimm-color-border-focus)`) are on border-color longhands. No mismatches found.

**🟡 PLAUSIBLE, needs a manual keyboard check — several new `variant="unstyled"` IconButtons define no explicit `_focusVisible`.** `leftBar/index.tsx:83-95` (hamburger), `rightBar/index.tsx:205-215` (tablet search), `:242-260` (account trigger), `:387-397` (mobile search), `:427-445` (mobile bag), `:452-464` (mobileL2 close) all omit `_focusVisible`. This is inconsistent with every *other* new interactive atom in this PR, which explicitly tokenizes it: `ZimmNavItem` (`zimmNavItem.css.ts:47-51`), `ZimmSearchInput`'s clear button (`index.tsx:103-106`), and `Header`'s own `logoButton` part (`header.css.ts:73-74`) all set `_focusVisible` via `var(--zimm-focus-ring)` explicitly. I could not confirm in a browser whether Chakra's base Button theme's default focus ring still applies under `variant="unstyled"` (in which case these get an un-tokenized, inconsistent ring) or not at all (a WCAG 2.4.7/2.4.11 gap) — flagging for a DevTools tab-through check.

**Recipe state exhaustiveness — open question, not a finding either way.** `ZimmNavItem` (the most-reused new interactive part: L1 triggers, mega-menu leaf links, drawer rows) defines `_hover`/`_focusVisible` but no `_active`/`_disabled`. SFCC-746 explicitly disclaims owning hover/focus/active states ("defined in UI kit, not re-specified in this ticket"), so I'm not treating this as an AC violation. I could not locate any Figma node reference in this PR's comments for a nav-item pressed/disabled state either way — I don't have Figma tool access in this session to check directly, so per the instructions I'm flagging this as an open question rather than asserting a gap.

---

## Angle 6 — Accessibility

**🔴 SFCC-747 AC10 violated — logo is not the first focusable element. CONFIRMED.**
`header/index.tsx` renders `topBar` (`LeftBar` — hamburger + desktop nav; then `RightBar` — search + icon buttons) at lines 230-251, **before** `logoBar` (the logo button) at lines 256-270. DOM/tab order therefore puts every nav item, the hamburger, the search input, and every icon button *ahead of* the logo. This isn't circumstantial — the PR's own test proves it:
```
overrides/app/components/header/index.test.tsx:107-117
test('is reachable via keyboard Tab order', ...) {
  // The topBar row's own controls (LeftBar's menu-control button, RightBar's close-icon
  // stub — see the mocks above) sit ahead of the logoBar's logo button in DOM order; tab
  // past both first, matching the real component tree.
  await user.tab(); await user.tab(); await user.tab();
  expect(screen.getByRole('button', {name: 'Logo'})).toHaveFocus();
}
```
The test passes *because* it encodes the AC-violating order as correct. The old header (pre-PR) had no such ordering constraint to violate since it wrapped the logo/nav differently — this is this PR's own layout decision.

**🔴 SFCC-747 AC9 violated — logo's accessible name is "Logo," not "Zimmermann, go to homepage." CONFIRMED.**
`header/index.tsx:258-259`:
```tsx
<Button aria-label={t('header.button.assistive_msg.logo', 'Logo')} variant="unstyled" onClick={onLogoClick} __css={styles.logoButton}>
  <ZimmLogo sx={HEADER_LOGO_SX} />
</Button>
```
`translations/en-US.json` confirms the shipped fallback is literally `"Logo"`. Because the wrapping `<Button>` carries its own explicit `aria-label`, `ZimmLogo`'s own `aria-label="Zimmermann"` (`zimmLogo/index.tsx:42`, on the inner `role="img"` SVG) is completely superseded in the accessible-name computation — a screen reader announces only "Logo, button," never "Zimmermann" and never the required destination phrase.

**🟡 New nested `<nav>` landmark — regression, not pre-existing. CONFIRMED.**
`header/leftBar/index.tsx:99`: `<chakra.nav __css={styles.nav}>{children}</chakra.nav>`. At tablet+, `children` resolves to `<ListMenu>`, which renders its own `<nav id="list-menu" aria-label="Main navigation">` (`list-menu.tsx:77`) — producing `<nav><nav aria-label="Main navigation">…</nav></nav>`. The pre-PR header wrapped the identical `children` in a plain `<Box {...styles.bodyContainer}>` (a `<div>`), confirmed via `git show 269d5d4:.../header/index.tsx:236` — so this nested-landmark structure is newly introduced by this PR's `leftBar.css.ts`/`chakra.nav` choice, not inherited.

**🟡 `PopoverFooter onClick` on a non-natively-interactive element with no `role`/keyboard handling of its own. CONFIRMED (rule-letter), likely low practical impact.**
`rightBar/index.tsx:304`: `<PopoverFooter onClick={handleSignout} cursor={isSigningOut ? 'not-allowed' : 'pointer'}>` — `PopoverFooter` isn't natively interactive and has neither `role` nor `tabIndex`/`onKeyDown` of its own, which is exactly what components.md's onClick-on-non-native rule exists to catch. In practice the inner `<Button>` (line 306) is a real, natively keyboard-operable element whose click (mouse or keyboard-triggered) bubbles up to `PopoverFooter`'s handler, so today this likely isn't a live keyboard-trap — but it's a fragile pattern (any future markup change that stops the click event bubbling, e.g. an intermediate wrapper, silently breaks sign-out with no compile-time signal), and it doesn't follow the rule as written.

**Clean:** every new `<Image>` has `alt` (sourced through `resolveImageEntry`'s defensive fallback chain); every new `IconButton` has `aria-label` (spot-checked all ~10); no raw `<div onClick>` pattern anywhere in the new code — every clickable non-button row goes through `ZimmNavItem`, which renders a real `<a>`/`<button>`.

---

## Angle 7 — Against the ticket

Verified against each AC:
- SFCC-52 AC1/2/6/7 — present (sticky container `header.css.ts:31-32`; RightBar's icon set matches AC6; LeftBar hamburger + RightBar mobileSection matches AC7).
- SFCC-747 AC1-7 (masthead placement) — structurally fine.
- SFCC-747 **AC9 and AC10 — both violated**, see Angle 6 above.
- SFCC-747 AC11 (visible focus ring, 3:1 contrast) on the logo itself — `logoButton`'s `_focusVisible`/`_focus` are present and tokenized (`header.css.ts:73-74`); I could not verify the actual rendered contrast ratio without a browser.
- SFCC-52 AC8/9/10/11 (mobile drawer open/close, categories, Saved/Account footer) — all confirmed implemented (`useHeaderMenuExpandedState`, `DrawerMenuL1Nav`, `DrawerMenuView`'s footer block).
- SFCC-96 (desktop mega-menu: left column, right promo image, Close control, Contentful-managed) — structurally present; promo images ship unoptimized (Angle 1 finding).
- SFCC-746 (Contentful-managed nav, region scoping) — `pickMostSpecificByRegion`/`filterByRegion` correctly reused/extended from the footer pattern; the ticket's own disclaimer on hover/focus/active states is respected by not holding this PR to that bar.

---

## Angle 8 — Intra-step DRY

**🔵 `'/login'` typed independently in two files, no shared constant.** `header/index.tsx:215` (`navigate('/login')`, post-signout redirect) vs. `drawer-menu/index.tsx:24` (`const SIGN_IN_HREF = '/login';`). Different use-cases but the same literal route with no shared source — a candidate for a small shared route-constants module, matching the `footerShared.ts`/`headerShared.ts` precedent this codebase already established. ONE-OFF today, UNIFORM-shaped risk (nothing stops a third file from re-typing it).

**Clean — breakpoints.** `BP` (from `theme/components/headerShared.ts`) is the single shared source consumed identically by `leftBar.css.ts`, `rightBar.css.ts`, and `megaMenuContent.css.ts` — this exactly matches the `footerShared.ts` reference pattern the rubric calls out.

**Clean — other candidate constants.** `HEADER_NAV_INCLUDE_DEPTH` and `MAXIMUM_NUMBER_COLUMNS` are each defined exactly once with no parallel literal found elsewhere.

All three reviews are in and cross-verified. Here's the full picture.

## Gate table — head vs base

| Gate | Base (`269d5d4`) | Head (`10eb79d`) | Net new from this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tsc --noEmit` | clean | clean | none |
| `lint` | 20 problems (4E/16W), all inherited | 24 problems (5E/19W) | 1 prettier error (new `useHeaderNav.test.ts`) + 6 warnings, all in new files |
| `audit:tokens` | 4 unacknowledged (all in the old header this PR replaces) | 1 unacknowledged | net **improvement**; the 1 new hit is `footer.css.ts:20`'s `'59.125em' // 946px` — no acknowledged-exception marker |
| `test` (vitest) | 408 tests / 26 files, all passing | 612 tests / 41 files, all passing | +204 tests, all green |
| Required CI checks that actually ran | — | Branch Target ✅, Unit tests ✅, Storybook a11y ✅ all green; Playwright/BrowserStack skipped (expected, change-scoping) | |
| Mergeable | — | GitHub says CONFLICTING | only in `.claude/registry/{components,hooks}.md`, both auto-generated — trivial, not a real conflict |
| Review state | — | `REVIEW_REQUIRED`, 0 unresolved threads | CodeRabbit's "Approved ✅" late in the thread is a chat reply, not a filed approval, and it predates the current head by one commit |

Mechanically this PR is in good shape. The findings below are everything the gates can't see.

## Findings, ranked by cost of ignoring

**1. `overrides/app/components/responsive/index.tsx` — new override, sitewide blast radius, unrelated to any of the 5 tickets.** CONFIRMED. Changes the mobile/desktop split used by `HideOnDesktop`/`HideOnMobile` from Chakra's default (`lg`, 992px) to `md` (768px). Because this repo's build resolver redirects *every* import of that base path, not just ones inside `overrides/`, this silently changes rendering on **10 real, active, un-overridden consumers**: the app shell itself (`_app/index.jsx`), PDP's `product-item`, PLP (`product-list/index.jsx`), `search/index.jsx` and its suggestions panel, `bonus-product-view-modal`, the DNT notice hook, and both checkout footers. None of this is reviewed, tested, or mentioned anywhere in the PR description. This is the single largest "something could quietly break on a page nobody was watching" risk in the whole diff.

**2. SFCC-747 AC10 violated — the logo is not the first focusable element.** CONFIRMED (I found this independently; zm-tester found it independently too, via the PR's *own test*, which asserts 3 Tab presses before the logo gets focus and documents in a comment that the nav/icons "sit ahead of the logoBar's logo button in DOM order"). `header/index.tsx` renders the entire nav + icon cluster before the logo in the DOM, with no `order`/`tabIndex` override anywhere in the tree to decouple tab order from visual order.

**3. SFCC-747 AC9 violated — the logo's accessible name is "Logo," never "Zimmermann."** CONFIRMED. The wrapping `<Button aria-label="Logo">` shadows the inner `<ZimmLogo aria-label="Zimmermann" role="img">` in standard accessible-name computation — a screen reader announces "Logo, button," not "Zimmermann, go to homepage."

**4. New nested `<nav>` landmark — genuine regression vs. the old header.** CONFIRMED, including the base-commit diff. `leftBar.css.ts`'s `chakra.nav` wraps `<ListMenu>`, which renders its own labeled `<nav>` — producing an unlabeled `<nav>` containing a labeled `<nav>`. The old header used a plain `<Box>` here.

**5. Mega-menu can get stuck open with a phantom "Close" control and no visible panel.** CONFIRMED via full trace (not just plausible) — a fast hover-then-close within ~2 animation frames hits a real gap between the motion reducer and its rAF-deferred value commit. Self-heals on the next hover, but no test at any layer (reducer or DOM-timing) exercises this interleaving.

**6. Mega-menu/drawer promo images ship full-resolution, unoptimized.** CONFIRMED. A complete, well-documented AVIF/WebP responsive-image builder (`contentfulImage.ts`) was built specifically for these images and has zero consumers — both actual call sites render the raw Contentful URL instead, against AGENTS.md's explicit performance rules.

**7. content.text:
**The two SFCC-747 violations, plain terms:**

**1. Tab order — logo should be first, but it's actually last.**
Picture using the site with a keyboard only, no mouse (this is how screen-reader users and many people with motor disabilities browse). You'd expect hitting Tab once to land on the logo, since it's the "take me home" element and the ticket explicitly requires it be first. Instead, right now, Tab takes you through the hamburger button, then all the nav links (New, Clothing, Accessories...), then Search, Account, Wishlist, and Bag — and only after all of that do you reach the logo. The PR's own test literally checks this and expects it: it does `Tab, Tab, Tab` and only then expects the logo to have focus.

Why did this happen despite the layout looking correct? The logo genuinely does sit visually below the nav bar (that part's right, and required). But browsers tab through elements in the order they appear in the *code*, not the order they appear on screen — and in the code, the developer wrote the nav bar first and the logo second. Nobody added the (fairly standard) trick to make it appear later but tab first.

**2. Accessible name — screen readers announce "Logo," not "Zimmermann."**
Screen readers read out a label for every button so a blind user knows what it does. The ticket says this one should announce "Zimmermann, go to homepage." There are actually two labels stacked here: an inner one on the logo graphic itself saying "Zimmermann," and an outer one on the button wrapping it saying just "Logo." When a button has its own label, screen readers use *only* that one and ignore anything inside it — so the "Zimmermann" label never gets heard at all. A screen reader user just hears "Logo, button."

Both are small code fixes once someone's aware of them, but as written they don't match what the ticket asks for.

**The responsive.tsx change, plain terms:**

There's one shared helper component used all over the site whose only job is "show this on mobile, hide it on desktop" (or vice versa). This PR changed where that line is drawn — the cutoff moves from 992px-wide screens down to 768px-wide screens. Anything in between (a fairly normal tablet or small-laptop window) used to count as "desktop" and will now suddenly count as "mobile" instead.

That helper isn't only used in the header. I checked, and it's also used on: the product page, the search results grid, the search suggestions dropdown, the "you might also like" popup, both checkout footers, a "do not track" popup, and the outer shell that wraps the entire site. None of those are part of this PR's actual job (they're not in any of the 5 tickets), but all of them quietly change behavior the moment this merges — and nothing in the PR mentions testing that, because nobody was looking at those pages while reviewing a "rebuild the header" PR.

Concrete example: today, someone on a 900px-wide window sees the desktop checkout footer. After this merges, without anyone touching checkout code, they'd see the mobile one instead.

Happy to go deeper on either, or we can move to the verdict calls whenever you're ready.

content.text:
**responsive.tsx — the exact mechanism, from source:**

Old (base SFCC), hardcoded:
```js
HideOnDesktop: display={{base: 'block', lg: 'none'}}   // visible 0–991px, hidden 992px+
HideOnMobile:  display={{base: 'none', lg: 'block'}}   // hidden 0–991px, visible 992px+
```
New (this PR):
```ts
const MOBILE_DESKTOP_SPLIT = 'md';  // was 'lg'
HideOnDesktop: display={{base: 'block', md: 'none'}}   // visible 0–767px, hidden 768px+
HideOnMobile:  display={{base: 'none', md: 'block'}}   // hidden 0–767px, visible 768px+
```
So concretely: at a window width of, say, 850px — under the old code that's still "mobile" (850 < 992), under the new code it's now "desktop" (850 ≥ 768). Anything using these two helpers flips which version it shows across that whole 768–991px band.

One thing I should've surfaced the first time: the developer did leave a reason, not a silent change — the code comment says the header/footer/mega-menu already switch at 768px (`md`), but this generic helper was still switching at 992px (`lg`), so in that 768–991px band, something wrapped in both helpers could end up hidden by both simultaneously — a real "dead zone" bug, not an arbitrary pick. That's a legitimate justification for *why* — it doesn't change that the 9 other pages inheriting it (PDP, PLP, search, checkout, etc.) weren't part of anyone's test plan for this PR.

**On the tab-order point — I want to push on this a bit rather than just drop it, because there's a real tension here:**

WCAG has a principle (2.4.3, "meaningful sequence") that generally says tab order *should* match visual/reading order — so nav-first-then-logo, matching what's visually on screen, is actually the *safer* default from that angle. Deliberately making the logo jump to first in tab order while staying visually second (which is what satisfying AC10 literally would require) is the kind of DOM/visual mismatch that's normally flagged as its *own* accessibility smell.

But the Jira ticket (SFCC-747, AC10) is explicit and unambiguous: *"Given a keyboard-only user is navigating the header, when they Tab to the logo, then the logo link is the first focusable element in the header, before any navigation items or icons."* I checked its full history — that's the only version of this AC that's ever existed, set once on 2026-08-14, never revised.

So: are you saying that AC is simply wrong/outdated and should be corrected in Jira (nav-first is the actual intended, correct behavior), or is there something else reconciling this I'm not seeing? I don't want to quietly drop a written, confirmed AC without your explicit call on it, but I also don't want to hold the PR to a requirement that's arguably fighting a more fundamental accessibility principle.

content.text:
They're not the same mechanism at all — and digging into this surfaced something more useful than the original question.

**Different code, no shared plumbing.** I checked: `footer.css.ts`'s 946px value has zero connection to `responsive.tsx`. It's a private constant (`BP_CONTENT_WRAP = '59.125em'`) used only in a raw CSS `@media` query inside `footer.css.ts` itself, controlling one specific thing — whether the site-map link columns sit beside the subscribe box or wrap underneath it. It never touches `HideOnDesktop`/`HideOnMobile` or the shared `md`/`lg` breakpoint keys `responsive.tsx` uses. The footer has always had its own separate breakpoint scheme (`BP.tablet`=768px, `BP.desktop`=1024px, defined in `footerShared.ts`), independent of the generic Chakra breakpoints. So these are two unrelated "breakpoint changes" that just happen to land in the same PR.

**There's a small irony worth knowing, though.** The `responsive.tsx` change justifies moving to 768px on the logic that "768px is already the line everywhere else — header, footer, mega-menu." But this PR's own footer work is doing the opposite in the same breath: the 946px comment says 768px specifically *didn't leave enough room* for the footer's site-map columns and subscribe box to sit side by side, so it needed its own separate, wider cutoff. Same PR, same general area, two different answers to "is 768 the right line" — not a contradiction exactly, just a sign that 768px isn't some universally correct number, it's just this design system's label for "tablet."

**The actually useful thing I found chasing this down:** `footerShared.ts` still defines `BP.tabletWide` (860px), and `footer.css.ts`'s `linksInner` block still uses it (`gap: 'var(--zimm-scale-5xl)'` at that width). That exact constant, in that exact file, is what **PR #69** — a separate, already-open, already-CodeRabbit-clean PR — is actively **deleting**, with the stated reason "it was our own invention, not a design constraint, and it was making the tablet footer worse." Same file, same style block, opposite direction. Whichever of #65 or #69 merges to `develop` second is going to either fail to compile (`BP.tabletWide` no longer exists) or silently resurrect the exact thing #69 is trying to remove. That's a real, concrete coordination problem between two live PRs — worth a heads-up to whoever owns #69 before either one merges, regardless of what we decide on #65.

message.content: what is the standard vs. what does the AC say? ELI5

content.text:
**The standard / common guidance:** Tab order should generally match what you see on the page, top to bottom. If the nav bar is drawn above the logo (which is a separate AC on this same ticket — AC2 — and nobody's disputing that one), then a keyboard user tabbing through nav first, then reaching the logo, matches the picture in front of them. That's the safer default accessibility guidance leans toward: don't make the tab order jump around relative to what's visually on screen, because it breaks the mental map a screen-reader user builds as things get announced.

**What this AC asks for:** the opposite, specifically for the logo. Even though the logo sits visually *below* the nav (per AC2), AC10 says it must still be the *first* thing you tab to — jumping ahead of the nav bar that's drawn above it.

So it's not just "unusual" — it's asking for a tab-order/visual-order mismatch, which is generally the specific pattern accessibility guidance cautions against, not a neutral stylistic choice. Put simply: **the standard says "tab order should match what's on screen"; this AC says "make an exception for the logo, and put it first anyway."** There's no reasoning written into the ticket for why that exception should exist — it just states the requirement.

I've now empirically measured the actual tab order at desktop width, and the logo lands at tab index 13, not 3 as I initially estimated from reading the code. My earlier "3 tabs" guess came from the PR's own test, which used a simplified mocked test harness with stub buttons instead of the real controls.

Looking closer at the sequence, I notice duplicate entries — Search and My Cart both appear twice in the tab order (indices 7 and 11, 10 and 12). This suggests some elements meant to be hidden at certain breakpoints are still present and focusable in the DOM, possibly because they're hidden via responsive display styles rather than a hard `display: none` I could filter out.

I'm now considering RightBar's structure: there's a desktop/tablet section with search and icons, and a separate mobile-only section with search and cart. If the mobile section's display isn't properly hidden at desktop widths, both sections could render simultaneously, explaining the duplicate Search/Cart entries at indices 7,10 and 11,12 — though I'd already thought I excluded elements with display:none directly on the button itself.

But I realize the flaw here: display:none on a parent wrapper doesn't propagate as computed display:none to its children, since CSS display isn't inherited — a button inside a hidden ancestor still reports its own default display value, not 'none', even though it never renders. So checking each element's own computed display property is insufficient; I actually need to verify rendered visibility using something like bounding rect dimensions or offsetParent, which properly accounts for hidden ancestors.

This means the two duplicate Search/Cart entries at indices 11 and 12 are likely false positives — mobile section buttons hidden behind a display:none ancestor that real keyboard Tab navigation would correctly skip. I should redo the check using offsetParent or rect area to get the true tab stop count, since excluding those two entries would shift Logo down to index 11 instead of 13.

content.thinking:
I notice there's no request for Contentful nav data here, and everything shown returned 200 or 404 with nothing pending. This log seems to just capture page load requests repeated three times, not something tied specifically to the hamburger click, so it might be capped and missing what I actually need.

There's a repeated 404 on the shopper-context endpoint, likely a known base-SFCC issue unrelated to this PR. The Contentful calls I saw errors for in the console aren't showing up here at all, which makes me think either they use a different fetch mechanism not captured by this log, or the log only retains the last 40 entries and the Contentful calls got pushed out earlier. Without evidence of a hanging network request tied to the click, I'm now leaning toward this being a JS-execution or rendering issue instead — something like an infinite loop or an expensive synchronous computation.

But it could also be a quirk of the automated browser tool's click simulation itself rather than a real product bug. Since I've reproduced this twice already, I want to test one more thing: try activating the hamburger button via keyboard (tab to it, then press Enter) instead of a simulated click, to see if the hang is specific to how left_click dispatches events or if it's a genuine app-level issue that happens regardless of interaction method.

content.thinking:
The dispatched click finished in about 1.2 milliseconds, essentially instant, which confirms the hang is specific to the tool's native click simulation rather than a genuine app bug — the React handler itself runs fast when triggered via JS. Still, the drawer immediately shows zero width and height even through this method, though that could just be an artifact of checking synchronously right away rather than a real issue.

Since state updates and CSS transitions take a moment to render, that same-microtask check wouldn't reflect the actual opening animation, so I want to wait briefly and re-check whether the drawer genuinely opens via JS click. This is a significant correction to my earlier finding — the 30-second hang and failure to open weren't a real app defect but likely a quirk of how the automation harness simulates mouse events during a full-screen transition, unrelated to how an actual user's tap would behave. I need to fix this before saying anything further to Marcel, so let me verify the drawer opens properly after a short wait.

## Full coverage complete — here's the consolidated report

**Correction first, since it's important:** the "hamburger hangs for 30s and never opens" finding from last message was **wrong** — and I want to own that clearly rather than bury it. I tracked it down: it was an artifact of my own testing tool's click-simulation, not the app. Triggering the exact same button via a direct JS click resolved in ~1ms and the drawer opened correctly. I'm glad I kept digging instead of leaving that as a real finding — it would have been the most alarming thing in this whole review, and it isn't real. Struck from the record.

### Confirmed working correctly
- **Mobile drawer, both levels.** L1 shows all 5 categories in the right order, hamburger correctly swaps to ×, Wishlist/Sign In sit below — matches spec. Drilling into "Clothing" shows the right subcategory list plus a real, loading promo image, with a back chevron replacing the hamburger. Clean.
- **Z.Immerse.** Confirmed via the actual DOM: it's a real `<a href="/immerse">`, while New/Clothing/Accessories/Collections are all drill-down buttons. Exactly matches the explicit requirement that Z.Immerse is a direct link, not a mega-menu trigger.
- **Tablet layout.** Icon order is Search→Account→Wishlist→Bag (search correctly leftmost), each a 24×24px touch target, logo correctly 627×74px matching Figma exactly at this breakpoint too.
- **Keyboard focus rings work in general** — confirmed real, visible outlines on nav items and footer links when reached via genuine Tab (not just claimed by the code, actually rendering).

### Confirmed problems (new, from hands-on testing)
- **Self-hosted fonts are failing to decode** (`OTS parsing error: invalid sfntVersion`) for both Futura Round files — the whole site is silently rendering in a fallback font, ~13% wider per this codebase's own docs. Not something PR #65 touched; looks like an environment/build issue specific to this preview. Still worth flagging since it undermines precise visual comparison until fixed.
- **Mega-menu stuck-open bug reproduces on a single, ordinary first click** — worse than "requires a fast double-interaction." One plain click from a fresh page load was enough.
- **AC9 (accessible name) and the nested `<nav>` landmark** — both independently confirmed live, exactly as the code review predicted.

### Genuinely inconclusive — needs your own eyes, not mine
- **What the mega menu actually looks like when open.** DOM/CSS say it renders correctly (right size, right content, right colors) — but my screenshot tool can't reliably capture Chakra's portal-positioned popovers, so I can't confirm the actual visual.
- **The missing-focus-ring buttons.** I tried several ways to get a clean keyboard-focus reading on the flagged tablet search icon and kept hitting my own tooling snags (accidental navigation, miscounted tab stops). I'm not going to force a confident answer here — this one needs a real person tabbing through it.

That's full coverage of what a browser can tell us. Ready for the verdict whenever you are, or happy to keep digging on anything specific.

content.text:
Let's start with #1 — the highest-priority item.

## What's actually happening

Every interactive element on a page has an "accessible name" — the text a screen reader speaks when it lands on that element. Normally that comes from whatever's visually inside it, or from an explicit `aria-label` if one's set.

Here, there are **two** labels stacked on the same control:
- The wrapping `<button>` has `aria-label="Logo"`
- The `<svg>` (the actual wordmark graphic) inside it has `aria-label="Zimmermann"` and `role="img"`

The rule browsers follow: if an element has its own `aria-label`, that's the end of the search — nothing inside it gets consulted at all. So the button's real, computed name is "Logo." The "Zimmermann" label sitting one level down is never reached.

**Where:** `overrides/app/components/header/index.tsx`, the `<Button aria-label={t('header.button.assistive_msg.logo', 'Logo')}>` wrapping `<ZimmLogo />`.

## How to confirm it yourself

**Fastest — Chrome DevTools, no screen reader needed:**
1. Open the PR preview: `https://zimmermann-pr-f52-3f524845.sfdc-8tgtt5-ecom1.exp-delivery.com/`
2. Right-click the "ZIMMERMANN" wordmark in the header → **Inspect**
3. In the Elements panel, with that `<button>` highlighted, look at the sidebar tabs on the right — there's an **Accessibility** tab (next to Styles/Computed/Layout). Click it.
4. Under "Computed Properties" it'll show `Name: "Logo"`. That's the confirmation — that's the literal string a screen reader would speak.

**More convincing — actually hear it, since you're on a Mac:**
1. Press **Cmd+F5** (or Cmd+Fn+F5 on newer keyboards) to turn on VoiceOver.
2. On the page, press **Tab** repeatedly until focus lands on the logo (it's the 10th stop from the top of the header — you'll pass all the nav items and icons first, which is the separate AC10 thing we already resolved).
3. Listen. It'll say **"Logo, button"** — not "Zimmermann."
4. Cmd+F5 again to turn VoiceOver back off.

Try either one (or both) and let me know what you get — then we'll move to #2.

content.text:
## What's actually happening

Screen reader users navigate by "landmarks" — nav, main, footer, etc. — the same way you'd use a table of contents. A dedicated shortcut lets them jump straight to "the navigation" without listening to everything in between.

This PR wraps the whole nav area in a `<nav>` element in `leftBar/index.tsx`. But the thing it wraps — `<ListMenu>` — *also* renders its own `<nav>` as its own root, already labeled "Main navigation." So the real DOM ends up as:

```html
<nav>                              ← added by this PR, no label
  <nav aria-label="Main navigation">  ← ListMenu's own, already existed
    ...
  </nav>
</nav>
```

One landmark nested inside another, same type, and the outer one is unlabeled. The old header didn't have this problem — it wrapped the same content in a plain `<div>` (via a `Box`), not a `<nav>`. So this is new, from this PR's `leftBar.css.ts` styling choice, not something inherited.

**Where:** outer one — `overrides/app/components/header/leftBar/index.tsx`, line ~99. Inner one — `overrides/app/components/list-menu/list-menu.tsx`, line ~77.

**Why it matters:** it's not going to crash anything, but it muddies the page's landmark structure — someone using "jump to navigation" gets an unlabeled region containing another, differently-labeled one, which isn't a meaningful structure to expose.

## How to confirm it yourself

**Fastest — browser console, one line:**
1. Open the preview, DevTools → Console tab
2. Paste: `document.querySelectorAll('nav').length` — should return `2`, not `1`
3. Then: `document.querySelectorAll('nav')[1].closest('nav') !== document.querySelectorAll('nav')[1]` — `true` confirms the second one is sitting inside the first

**Visual — DevTools Elements panel:** inspect the nav area, and just look at the indentation in the tree — you'll see `<nav>` as a parent, and another `<nav aria-label="Main navigation">` indented inside it.

**Landmark-by-landmark, the way a screen reader user would experience it:** VoiceOver on, then **VO+U** to open the Rotor, arrow over to "Landmarks." You'll see two "navigation" entries where there should logically be one — one with no name at all.

Try whichever's easiest, and I'll walk you through #3 (the mega-menu stuck-open bug) when you're ready.

Good question — and the answer is genuinely elegant. Found it in the code, quoting the actual comment because it explains a subtlety worth seeing:

**The mechanism:** `megaMenuContent/index.tsx` sets `tabIndex={isFullyOpen ? undefined : -1}` on every leaf link. `list-menu-popover.tsx` feeds that prop with `isFullyOpen={phase === 'open'}` — tied directly to the same open/close animation state machine from bug #3. So the links only become real Tab stops once the phase machine reaches `'open'` — its fully-settled resting state, not just "started opening."

**Why it needs to work this way, not just via CSS:** the developer's own comment explains it well:

> "...a 0-height/overflow-hidden ancestor does NOT reliably remove a real `<a>`/`<button>` descendant from the Tab order on its own, only from view. Without this, Tab pressed quickly after opening could land focus on a link that was still invisible (WCAG 2.4.7)."

In plain terms: CSS that visually hides a panel (height 0, clipped overflow) doesn't actually stop a browser from tabbing INTO a link sitting inside it — it just makes that link invisible while still technically reachable. So without this explicit `tabIndex` toggle, someone tabbing fast right as a menu opens could land on a link they can't see yet. This `isFullyOpen` gate exists specifically to prevent that.

So: this one's solid, deliberate engineering — not a bug, unrelated to #2 or #3. Good catch to double check it, but nothing to flag here.

content.text:
## What's actually happening

Opening the mega menu is animated: the panel grows from 0 height to full height, then its content fades in. That's tracked by a small state machine with phases — roughly `closed → expanding → open`, and the reverse on close.

There's a deliberate ~30ms delay (two animation frames) before the "real" target height actually gets applied — built specifically to fix a *different*, earlier flicker bug.

**The problem:** if you close the menu within that same ~30ms window — before the "opening" height has actually been applied yet — the code recalculates the "closing" target height. But since opening never actually applied its own change yet, the currently-set height and the new "closing" target end up being the *exact same number*. React sees "you're setting this to what it already is" and does nothing — no re-render, no CSS transition ever starts.

The "did it finish animating" signal comes entirely from that CSS transition completing. Since it never starts, the state machine gets stuck mid-close, permanently. Meanwhile, a separate, independent piece of code — the header's icon cluster — is watching a different flag that *did* update correctly, so it correctly swaps to "Close ×" — even though the panel itself never actually became visible.

**Where:** `overrides/app/hooks/useMegaMenuMotion.ts` (the state machine) working against `list-menu-popover.tsx`'s `useTransitionSafeValue` (the ~30ms deferral).

## How to try it yourself

1. Load the preview **fresh** each attempt: `https://zimmermann-pr-f52-3f524845.sfdc-8tgtt5-ecom1.exp-delivery.com/`
2. Click (or hover) "Clothing" in the top nav
3. Check: does "Close ×" appear top-right where Search/Account/Wishlist/Bag were? Is there *nothing* showing below the nav bar?
4. **This is timing-sensitive — a genuine race, not guaranteed every single time.** I hit it on both of my attempts, but if a slow deliberate hover doesn't trigger it, try a quick, ordinary click instead — that's what worked for me.
5. Objective check, DevTools console: `document.querySelector('[aria-label="Clothing menu"]').getBoundingClientRect().height` — `0` while "Close" is showing confirms it. A real number (I saw `754` when it opened correctly) means it's fine.
6. To exit the stuck state: hover any nav item again — it should immediately recover. That's the self-healing part.

Give it a try — a couple of fresh reloads should be enough to catch it. Let me know what you get.

content.text:
Let me try that again, simpler.

Think of the mega menu as having **two separate things** that happen when you click a category:
1. A **light switch** in the header (shows "Close ×" instead of the icons)
2. An actual **door** that's supposed to swing open (the dropdown panel with the links)

Normally both happen together — you flip the switch, the door opens. Here's the sequence when it breaks:

1. You click "Clothing." The switch flips to "Close ×" immediately.
2. The door is *told* to start opening — but there's a tiny built-in pause (a fraction of a second) before it actually starts moving.
3. If you move your mouse away (or click again) during that tiny pause — before the door has physically moved at all — the app says "okay, close the door."
4. But the door never actually left "closed" in the first place. So "close the door" really means "move it from closed... to closed." Nothing moves.
5. The app only knows a door-movement finished by watching the door actually swing — and since it never moved, that "finished" signal never comes.
6. So the app gets stuck thinking "I'm still in the middle of closing," forever — until you hover a category again, which resets it.

**The visible result:** the switch says "open" (you see "Close ×"), but the door never moved (no dropdown ever appears). You're stuck looking at a Close button with nothing to close.

That's the whole bug — a timing gap between "the switch flips" and "the door actually moves," where closing too fast catches the door before it's left its starting position.

content.text:
Reproduced exactly what you found — and it's a more serious bug than what I originally traced. Here's the precise evidence:

After your hover+Escape pattern, I checked the computed state of all four category panels directly. "Clothing" showed:
```
height: 754px   ← the correct, fully-open value
opacity: 1       ← fully visible
visibility: hidden   ← but this stays hidden regardless
```

That `height: 754` is the exact right answer — the same number Figma specifies for this panel. **The animation actually finished correctly.** But something else — a separate, outer "is this popover open" flag that Chakra's own popover component manages — is stuck saying "hidden," and that flag wins no matter what the animation underneath it did correctly.

So there are really **two separate trackers** for "is the menu open," not one:
1. The custom animation state I explained earlier (height/opacity) — this one does have self-healing logic, hovering resets it.
2. Chakra's own built-in "is this popover open" state — this is the one your Escape-key pattern breaks, and **it has no self-healing logic at all.**

I tested hovering three different categories after triggering it, and none recovered — it stayed broken for all of them, exactly as you found. That matches your report precisely: not a per-item glitch, the whole mega-menu system gets stuck for the rest of the session.

This changes the severity read. What I originally described was "an occasional, self-healing hiccup if you close within a narrow timing window." What you actually found is "an ordinary keyboard interaction — hovering around and hitting Escape a few times — can permanently wedge the entire mega-menu until the page reloads." That's a meaningfully worse bug, and a more plausible way for a real shopper to hit it than what I'd described. Good catch — this needs to go back to the author as a bigger deal than my first pass suggested.

content.text:
Now I've actually traced it, not just theorized — and found something concrete. Let me explain what's really going on.

## Why this keeps happening — the real root cause

This one feature has **three separate systems**, each independently convinced it owns "is the menu open":

1. **Our own custom reducer** (`useMegaMenuMotion`) — tracks which item is active and what animation phase it's in.
2. **A custom timing hack** (`useTransitionSafeValue`) — deliberately delays applying the "real" height by ~30ms, bolted on to fix a *different*, earlier bug where the CSS transition wouldn't animate at all.
3. **Chakra's own built-in Popover component** — has its *own* internal open/close lifecycle: it repositions itself, manages where focus returns to, and — this is the piece I just confirmed — **has its own built-in Escape-key handling, switched on by default, that this code never turns off.**

I found the smoking gun. There's a comment in `megaMenuContent/index.tsx` that says, verbatim: *"Escape is not handled here — Chakra's Popover already closes on Escape from anywhere within its content (`closeOnEsc`, on by default)."* That's a deliberate choice — rely on Chakra's built-in behavior instead of writing it themselves.

But there's *also* a separate, hand-written Escape handler on the trigger button itself, in `list-menu-trigger.tsx`, doing the same job.

So pressing Escape can fire **two different "close this" paths for the same keypress** — the app's own reducer action, and Chakra's own internal one. And since each of the 5 nav categories is its own separate Chakra Popover component (all sharing one piece of shared app state), rapidly hovering across several of them while hitting Escape means you're firing both of these paths across *multiple independent components* in quick succession. When Chakra's own internal bookkeeping for one of those components doesn't finish settling before the next hover starts, it can get stuck believing it's positioned as closed — and simply telling it "you should be open" again later doesn't necessarily un-stick it, because from its own internal perspective, nothing new happened.

**In plain terms:** two different systems both think they're in charge of closing the menu, they don't fully coordinate with each other, and there are five separate copies of one of those systems all sharing one steering wheel. That combination is exactly the shape of bug that produces "sometimes it just doesn't come back."

## How to actually fix it

This isn't a one-line patch, but there's a clear direction, roughly in priority order:

1. **Stop letting Chakra handle Escape at all.** Set `closeOnEsc={false}` on the Popover, and route *every* Escape press through the one custom handler that already exists — which means adding an Escape handler to the panel content too (currently deliberately skipped, per that comment), since a user can have focus inside the panel, not just on the trigger button. One path instead of two removes the double-handling entirely.
2. **Make the reducer not depend on a browser event that might never fire.** Right now, "I finished closing" only gets recognized via a CSS `transitionend` event — and if nothing actually visually changed (the original bug), that event never comes. It needs a way to recognize "there was nothing to animate" and immediately finish the transition itself, instead of waiting on a signal that isn't coming.
3. **Add a simple lock so a new hover/close can't land in the middle of a transition still in flight.** Right now, a fast enough sequence of interactions can always find some timing gap. A brief "ignore new requests until the current one settles" guard closes that gap structurally, rather than chasing each specific race one at a time.

Point 1 is the one I'd hand to Tim first — it's concrete, it's exactly what the code's own comment shows was a conscious tradeoff, and it directly explains what you reproduced. Points 2 and 3 are more architectural and probably need his own time with it rather than a quick fix.

## What's actually happening

Someone built a genuinely careful, well-tested image pipeline — `overrides/app/utils/contentfulImage.ts` — specifically for these promo images. It's worth seeing what it actually does, because it's good work that just never got connected:

- Takes the raw Contentful image URL and a target size, and builds a proper `srcset`: AVIF (a modern, much smaller format) as the first choice, WebP as the fallback for browsers that don't support AVIF, each with a real 1x and 2x (retina) version.
- Uses Contentful's own CDN resizing (`?w=862&h=690&fit=fill&fm=avif&q=65` — Contentful can crop/resize/reformat images live via URL parameters).
- The crop behavior was specifically tuned against real production photos — an earlier version used face-detection cropping and it kept cutting off models' heads, so that got deliberately turned off in favor of a plain center-crop that tested reliably across every real asset.
- Quality settings (AVIF q65, WebP q95) were tuned to stay under a 300-400KB ceiling while still looking clean.

None of that ever runs. The actual code (`megaMenuContent/index.tsx`, `drawer-menu/index.tsx`) just does `<Image src={promoImage.src}>` — and `promoImage.src` is the *raw* Contentful URL with zero query params, which you already saw yourself in your own DevTools paste: `header-nav-new-promo.png`, no `?w=`, no `?fm=`, nothing. That's the browser downloading Contentful's full original master file — sized and encoded for whatever the source photo shoot delivered, not for a small lazy-loaded dropdown panel.

**Why it matters:** this is the exact thing AGENTS.md calls out directly — "never render full-resolution images at thumbnail size" — and mobile page speed is called out as a top project priority. A menu that only opens on hover/click downloading a full-size master image on every category is a real, avoidable cost.

## How to see the real difference yourself — no code change needed

Contentful's resizing works purely through URL parameters, so you can prove the savings live, on the actual current preview, without touching any code:

1. Open DevTools → Network tab, filter to "Img"
2. Open the "New" or "Clothing" mega menu, find the promo image request, check its size — that's what's shipping today
3. Now open the **same image URL** in a new browser tab, but add the exact parameters the dead pipeline would have used: append `?w=862&h=690&fit=fill&fm=webp&q=95` to the URL (862×690 is the panel's real size, pulled straight from `megaMenuContent.css.ts`)
4. Compare the file size DevTools reports for that second request against the first

That side-by-side is the actual, real-world size of the problem — not a theoretical estimate.

## Why the base-path import exists at all

This whole codebase is built on top of Salesforce's template code (sitting in `node_modules`), and Zimmermann customizes it by dropping same-named replacement files into `overrides/`. There's a build-time trick — a webpack plugin — that quietly redirects any import of the Salesforce path to Zimmermann's override instead, *if one exists*. That trick exists specifically so Salesforce's own original code (which has no idea Zimmermann's overrides exist) can keep importing things the normal way and still transparently get the customized version.

Think of it like a phone number with call-forwarding secretly set up on the office switchboard: dial the generic Salesforce number from an office phone, and it forwards you to Zimmermann's actual desk. But that forwarding rule only lives on *that one switchboard* — it's a webpack thing. Storybook and Vitest are different phone systems entirely; they don't know that forwarding rule exists. Dial the same generic number from either of those, and you just reach the generic Salesforce operator, full stop.

## Why that matters here specifically

There are genuinely two different situations:

1. **You're writing an override file that's standing in for a Salesforce file, and it needs something else Salesforce's original also needed.** Here, dialing the generic number is *correct* — you're pretending to be the original file, so you should behave like it.
2. **You're writing something new that just wants to reach a component that Zimmermann has already customized.** Here, you should dial Zimmermann's direct line — the relative import — because there's no reason to gamble on the switchboard trick working. It's needlessly fragile.

This barrel file (`list-menu/index.ts`) is brand new — it didn't exist before this PR. It's not pretending to be a Salesforce file; it's a convenience file Zimmermann's own code is meant to use. That's situation 2. And it already *knows* this — two of its four lines correctly dial the direct line (`ListMenu`, `ListMenuTrigger`). The third line, for no apparent reason, dials the generic switchboard number instead, for a component that has a direct line sitting right there.

**So the "wrongness" isn't that base-path imports are bad.** They're the right tool for situation 1. This is situation 2, the barrel already proves it knows that on two other lines, and the one line that doesn't follow its own pattern is the bug — it works today by accident (because the real app happens to have that switchboard trick running), and would silently fail the moment anyone tests or previews it somewhere that trick doesn't exist.

content.thinking:
Escape does work here — the drawer closes fully and the homepage returns with the hamburger icon restored. So there's technically a keyboard exit, meaning this isn't a strict WCAG 2.1.2 no-keyboard-trap violation, but it's still a serious bug: Tab alone can't reach the visible Close button, Back button, Search, or Bag controls while the drawer is open.

A keyboard user relying only on Tab (not knowing about Escape) would be stuck cycling through just the 12 category links, unable to reach controls they can clearly see on screen — a real WCAG 2.4.3/2.1.1 gap even with Escape as a technical workaround. I now have a solid, verified picture: focus cycles through exactly those 12 links in a closed loop, never reaching the chevron, close, search, or bag icons, though Escape closes the drawer entirely.

The root cause is architectural — those header icons are technically part of the persistent header component, not the Modal's own DOM content, confirmed via containment checks, even though visually they appear integrated into the drawer's top bar. Chakra's Modal correctly traps focus to its own content only, so anything outside it gets excluded from the tab sequence regardless of visual placement, meaning a mouse user can still click Close/Search/Bag while a keyboard-only user cannot reach them without knowing to press Escape instead. This turns out to be a more significant, newly-confirmed bug than the original focus-ring question I set out to check, which turned out to be a non-issue.

I should update Marcel on both: closing out the original focus-ring question as resolved (rings do show correctly on reachable items), and presenting this new finding clearly with its own root-cause explanation, then update the review notes file to reflect both changes.

For the fix direction, Chakra's default `trapFocus` needs to somehow also cover the header's Close/Search/Bag/Back controls — either by restructuring so those controls render inside the modal's own content tree, or by finding a way to extend the trap boundary across two separate DOM subtrees, which Chakra doesn't easily support out of the box.

Rather than committing to one exact fix without deeper investigation, I think the responsible approach is to clearly present the confirmed bug with solid evidence, explain the likely architectural cause, and flag that the precise implementation still needs more scoping.

Now I'll update the review notes file and put together a comprehensive report back to Marcel.

content.text:
Good news first: #6 (the focus rings) is resolved — you confirmed all four are fine with real Tab, so that's closed out as a non-issue.

But what you found while checking it is real, and worse. I put it through a rigorous check — pressed Tab from a clean drawer state and counted: focus cycles through exactly the 12 category links (Dresses → ... → All Clothing) and then **loops straight back to Dresses**. It never once reaches the back chevron, the ×, search, or bag icons — confirmed both by watching real Tab presses and by directly checking whether those buttons live inside the drawer's own DOM boundary. They don't.

One important nuance: **Escape does close the drawer.** So this isn't a total dead-end — there's a way out. But Tab is how most keyboard users actually navigate, and right now it silently skips four controls that are sitting right there on screen looking completely usable.

**Why:** those icons belong to the persistent header component, not to the drawer's own content. The drawer opens as a proper modal dialog, and modals are supposed to trap keyboard focus to their own content only — that's a correct, deliberate accessibility feature, not a bug in itself. The problem is that these icons were styled to visually look like they belong to the drawer's top bar, but they were never actually moved inside the boundary the modal traps focus to. So the trap is doing its job correctly; it's just trapping around the wrong boundary.

**Fix:** this one doesn't have a clean one-line answer like the others — it's a real design decision for Tim: either move those controls to genuinely render inside the drawer's own content, or restructure the focus trap to span both. Worth flagging clearly, but not something I'd hand him a diff for.

Updated in the notes. Want to keep going — #7, or the remaining "worth a comment" items?
